author: anishmoonka
name: Anish Moonka
text:
The column of ice in this video is hollow, and the liquid pouring down inside it is around minus 20 Celsius, colder than a home freezer, yet it stays liquid. It sinks because it is heavier than the seawater around it, freezing the ocean solid in its wake and killing nearly everything it reaches at the bottom. The nickname for it is the icy finger of death.

It is called a brinicle, short for brine icicle. When seawater freezes at the surface, the ice crystals push out their salt, because salt does not fit into the structure of ice. That rejected salt collects into pockets of leftover water that is both extremely salty and extremely cold. Salt lowers the freezing point of water, so even brine this cold keeps flowing.

As it sinks through cracks in the ice, the brine meets ordinary, less salty seawater and freezes it solid around the descending column. That builds a fragile hollow pipe, with the brine still running through the middle and freezing fresh ice at the tip. It can grow a couple of centimeters a minute.

When it reaches the bottom, the cold spreads sideways in a creeping web of ice. Starfish, sea urchins, and sea snails are too slow to crawl away, and they freeze where they sit. The Frozen Planet team came back from one dive to find a river of ice already laid across the seabed, with animals locked inside it.

Scientists had known about these since the 1960s, and the oceanographer Seelye Martin worked out how they form in 1974, even growing his own in a tank in his Seattle lab. No one had filmed one taking shape until 2011. That footage came from a BBC crew camped under the Antarctic ice, who fought off a seal that kept knocking over their cameras and caught a single brinicle building itself over about five to six hours.
